title: Photons and energy
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:42Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest card, phys-photons, teaches E = hf and frequency versus brightness but not how a photon's energy is split between freeing an electron and its kinetic energy, and the photoelectric card covers the effect without the energy balance at the depth this point needs, so a new point is the safer match.

draft.title: Photons and energy
card: Light comes in packets of energy called photons. One photon carries energy E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency of the light.
A higher frequency means more energy per photon. The intensity of a beam sets how many photons arrive each second, not the energy of each one.
In the photoelectric effect, one photon gives all its energy to one electron. Part of that energy frees the electron from the metal.
The rest of the energy becomes the electron's kinetic energy. So photon energy = energy to free the electron + kinetic energy.
draft.remember: One photon has energy hf. It goes into freeing one electron and the rest into its motion.

a.q: Light of frequency f is replaced by light of a higher frequency. The number of photons per second stays the same. What changes for each photon?
opts: Its speed in a vacuum is larger
a.why: Photon energy is E = hf, so a higher frequency gives each photon more energy. The number of photons per second is the intensity, and it has not changed. Light in a vacuum keeps the same speed whatever its frequency.
a.clue: Look at what E = hf depends on.

b.q: Violet light shines on a metal and ejects electrons. Only the number of photons per second is then doubled, and the frequency is unchanged. What happens to the kinetic energy of each ejected electron?
opts: It stays the same, but more electrons are ejected
It doubles, because the beam carries twice the energy
It halves, because the photons share their energy
It falls, because the electrons must share the energy
b.why: Each photon still has energy hf, and each gives all of it to one electron. Doubling the photons ejects more electrons but does not change the energy each one gets. The beam carries more energy in total, but no single electron receives it.
b.clue: One photon gives its energy to one electron.

b.best: It stays the same, but more electrons are ejected
